title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS STILL SPEAK IN TONGUES TODAY?
paragraphs:
SHOULD CHRISTIANS STILL SPEAK IN TONGUES TODAY?
What If Both Sides Have Been Asking the Wrong Question?
There is a sentence in the New Testament that should make both the skeptic and the enthusiast uncomfortable.
Not because it is confusing.
Because it is painfully clear.
“Do not forbid speaking in tongues.”
Those words did not come from a modern Pentecostal preacher. They were not written by someone trying to manufacture an emotional church service. They came from the apostle Paul.
And yet the same Paul who wrote those words also spent an extraordinary amount of time correcting the way spiritual gifts were being used.
That tension matters.

Because somewhere between the Christian who says, “Tongues are fake,” and the Christian who implies, “If you do not speak in tongues, you do not really have the Holy Spirit,” Scripture stands in the middle and refuses to surrender to either extreme.
So before defending your tradition, your denomination, your experience, your lack of experience, or the church culture that formed you, there is a more uncomfortable question:
What does the Bible actually say?
And even deeper than that...
Are we willing to obey Scripture if its answer unsettles our camp?
The New Testament word translated “tongue” is γλῶσσα — glōssa. Literally, it can refer to the physical tongue, but it can also mean a language. That matters immediately when we arrive at Pentecost.
Acts 2:4 reads:
“καὶ ἐπλήσθησαν πάντες Πνεύματος Ἁγίου, καὶ ἤρξαντο λαλεῖν ἑτέραις γλώσσαις...”
Kai eplēsthēsan pantes Pneumatos Hagiou, kai ērxanto lalein heterais glōssais...
“And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues...”
The phrase ἑτέραις γλώσσαις — heterais glōssais — means “other tongues” or “other languages.”
And Luke does not leave us guessing about what happened.
People from different regions heard the disciples speaking in their own languages.
The miracle was not meaningless noise.
God was making Himself known.
Men and women heard “the mighty works of God.”
Think about that.
Humanity had languages, borders, ethnic divisions, histories, rivalries, and wounds. Then the Spirit came, and suddenly the mighty works of God were being proclaimed across linguistic boundaries.
Pentecost was never primarily about making Christians look spiritually impressive.
It was about making Christ known.
That single truth already exposes something in us.
Because whenever a spiritual gift becomes more useful for displaying the spirituality of the believer than displaying the glory of Jesus, something has gone terribly wrong.
Paul later addresses tongues extensively in 1 Corinthians 12–14. And Corinth was not exactly the picture of spiritual maturity.
They had gifts.
They also had division.
They had knowledge.
They also had pride.
They had manifestations.
They also had disorder.
They could be spiritually impressive and spiritually immature at the same time.
That should terrify anyone who believes supernatural experiences automatically prove spiritual maturity.
They do not.
Jesus Christ is not impressed by our ability to appear spiritual.
The question is what the Spirit is producing in us.
Are we becoming more loving?
More holy?
More humble?
More obedient?
More forgiving?
More Christlike?
Because Paul deliberately places one of the most famous passages about love right in the middle of his discussion of spiritual gifts.
We often pull 1 Corinthians 13 out for weddings.
Paul wrote it to a church fighting over spirituality.
“If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.”
Imagine possessing extraordinary spiritual gifts...
and heaven hearing nothing but noise.
That is sobering.
You could impress a room and still grieve God with your pride.
You could defend the gifts of the Spirit while displaying very little fruit of the Spirit.
You could speak mysteriously in worship and then use the same mouth to destroy someone through gossip.
You could raise your hands on Sunday and refuse to forgive on Monday.
You could argue passionately that supernatural gifts still exist while quietly tolerating sin Jesus died to deliver you from.
And you could stand on the opposite side too.
You could know theology.
You could explain Greek grammar.
You could expose counterfeit manifestations.
You could mock emotional Christianity.
You could pride yourself on discernment...
and still have a heart frozen toward God.
Neither emotionalism nor intellectualism can save you.
Jesus saves.
That is why this discussion must never become a contest between charismatic Christians and cessationist Christians.
It must become a journey back to Scripture.

Some Christians believe miraculous sign gifts such as tongues belonged especially to the apostolic foundation of the early church and therefore ceased as that foundational era came to completion. Others believe the New Testament gives no explicit statement that tongues would cease before Christ's return and therefore understand the gift as potentially continuing until then.
Both positions have been defended by Christians who affirm the authority of Scripture.
But sometimes one verse becomes the battlefield.
First Corinthians 13:8 says:
“Ἡ ἀγάπη οὐδέποτε πίπτει... εἴτε γλῶσσαι, παύσονται...”
Hē agapē oudepote piptei... eite glōssai, pausontai...
“Love never fails... as for tongues, they will cease...”
The word παύσονται — pausontai — means they “will cease.”
So yes.
Scripture explicitly says tongues will cease.
The disagreement is not really over whether they cease.
The disagreement concerns when.
Paul continues:
“For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.”

Some cessationist interpretations have associated “the perfect” with the completion or maturity of the church’s revelatory foundation. Many continuationist interpreters understand it as the consummation associated with Christ’s return, especially because Paul soon says:
“For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face.”
Whatever position you adopt, humility is necessary because Paul’s central point is larger than winning an argument about spiritual gifts.
Gifts are temporary.
Love belongs to eternity.
There will come a day when nobody needs prophecy.
Nobody needs tongues.
Nobody needs partial knowledge.
Because faith will become sight.
The wounded hands of Jesus will be before us.
And suddenly many arguments that consumed Christians on earth will look very small beside the Lamb who was slain.
But until that day, what should Christians do?
Here is where another Greek sentence refuses to disappear.
Paul concludes his extended discussion in 1 Corinthians 14:39:
“ζηλοῦτε τὸ προφητεύειν, καὶ τὸ λαλεῖν μὴ κωλύετε γλώσσαις.”
Zēloute to prophēteuein, kai to lalein mē kōlyete glōssais.
“Earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.”
Do not forbid it.
But keep reading.
Because Paul does not say, “Therefore anything that happens in a worship service and is called spiritual must be accepted.”
Quite the opposite.
He regulates it.
He insists that corporate worship should build up the church.
He distinguishes private edification from intelligible congregational edification.
He says that if someone speaks publicly in a tongue, interpretation is necessary.
He limits how many should speak.
He says they should speak one at a time.
And if there is no interpreter?
Silence.
That does not sound like uncontrolled spiritual chaos.
It sounds like Spirit-governed order.
Paul eventually says:
“Let all things be done decently and in order.”
That means “the Holy Spirit made me do it” cannot become an excuse for disobeying instructions the Holy Spirit Himself inspired.
Think about that carefully.
The Spirit who gives gifts is the same Spirit who gave Scripture.
The Holy Spirit will never need you to violate the Word He inspired in order to prove that He is present.
So should Christians speak in tongues today?
Scripture gives us several boundaries that cannot honestly be ignored.
Tongues were genuinely present in the New Testament church.
They were a gift of the Holy Spirit.
Not every believer possessed the same gift.
Paul refused to forbid tongues.
Public use required order and, in the circumstances Paul describes, interpretation.
Spiritual gifts were intended to build others up rather than elevate the person possessing them.
And no spiritual gift can replace love, holiness, truth, repentance, or allegiance to Jesus Christ.
Those boundaries matter because there are painful abuses associated with this subject.
Some believers have been told that unless they speak in tongues, they do not have the Holy Spirit.
Paul's own teaching about the diversity of gifts makes that claim difficult to sustain.
In 1 Corinthians 12 Paul asks a sequence of rhetorical questions:
“Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues?”
The expected answer is no.
The body has many members.
The Spirit distributes gifts according to His will.
Your salvation does not rest upon whether you have spoken in tongues.
Your salvation rests upon Jesus Christ.
His incarnation.
His sinless life.
His cross.
His blood.
His resurrection.
His grace.
His promise.
If you belong to Christ, you do not need to manufacture an experience to make yourself acceptable to God.
You need Jesus.
Maybe somebody pressured you.
Maybe everyone around you seemed to experience something you did not.
Maybe you stood in a church service while people prayed over you and whispered inside:
“God... what is wrong with me?”
Listen carefully.
Do not fake something to impress Christians.
God already knows what is real.
You do not need borrowed syllables.
You do not need spiritual theater.
You need truth.
And if God gives a gift, you do not need to manufacture what God is perfectly capable of giving.
But perhaps your story is the opposite.
Maybe you have experienced something you sincerely believe was from the Holy Spirit, and somebody mocked you for it.
Your responsibility is not to retaliate.
Your responsibility is to test everything by Scripture.
Experiences do not interpret the Bible.
The Bible judges our experiences.
If something is genuinely from God, it does not need dishonesty to defend it.
And if something is false, calling it “spiritual” will not make it holy.
This is where the question about tongues becomes something much deeper.
Because maybe your greatest spiritual problem has nothing to do with tongues.
Maybe you speak beautifully in church but brutally to your spouse.
Maybe you can debate spiritual gifts but cannot remember the last time you wept over your sin.
Maybe you know exactly why another denomination is wrong but have become almost completely blind to the pride growing inside your own heart.
Maybe you want supernatural power without supernatural holiness.
Maybe you want manifestations without mortification of sin.
Maybe you want gifts without the Giver.
And Jesus is standing at the center of this entire conversation saying:
Come back to Me.
Because Christianity was never about tongues.
Christianity was never about cessationism.
Christianity was never about continuationism.
Christianity is about Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Buried.
Risen.
Reigning.
Returning.
The Holy Spirit was not sent to create celebrities out of Christians.
Jesus said the Spirit would glorify Him.
That becomes one of the safest questions we can ask about anything claiming to be spiritual:
Does this magnify Jesus?
Does it agree with Scripture?
Does it build up His people?
Does it produce humility?
Does it move sinners toward repentance?
Does it produce love?
Does it make Christ precious?
Or does it make the person with the microphone impressive?
Because there is something far more frightening than never speaking in tongues.
It is speaking Christian language your entire life while never truly knowing Christ.
You can learn the vocabulary.
You can learn when to raise your hands.
You can learn how Christians talk.
You can learn theology.
You can learn worship culture.
You can learn charismatic culture.
You can learn Reformed culture.
You can learn Baptist culture.
You can learn Pentecostal culture.
And still hide from Jesus.
That is the scandal beneath the argument.
We keep asking which gifts we possess while Jesus keeps confronting who possesses our hearts.
The Gospel begins by stripping away our performance.
All have sinned.
All fall short.
The charismatic needs grace.
The cessationist needs grace.
The preacher needs grace.
The theologian needs grace.
The person praying quietly in the last pew needs grace.
And the Savior gives grace to sinners who could never earn it.
Jesus took our guilt to the cross.
He carried the judgment our sin deserved.
He died.
And the grave could not keep Him.
That is where every spiritual gift must ultimately point.
Not to us.
To Him.
So if God has genuinely given you a spiritual gift, use it humbly.
If you believe certain gifts have ceased, hold that conviction from Scripture rather than contempt for Christians who disagree.
If you are unsure, keep studying.
Do not be frightened by the question.
Open the Bible.
Read Acts.
Read 1 Corinthians 12, 13, and 14 together rather than building your theology from isolated verses.
Pray.
Ask God for wisdom.
Test claims.
Reject manipulation.
Reject counterfeit spirituality.
Reject spiritual pride.
And above everything...
cling to Jesus.
Because someday tongues will cease.
Prophecies will end.
Our partial knowledge will give way to something infinitely greater.
But love never fails.
And when you finally see Jesus face to face, you will not regret one moment spent pursuing truth with humility.
Maybe this article exposed something in you.
Pride.
Fear.
Confusion.
A wound from church.
A counterfeit experience you have been afraid to question.
Or perhaps an arrogance that made you dismiss brothers and sisters before genuinely hearing them.
Do not hide behind another theological argument.
Bring it to Christ.
Someone reading quietly may need your testimony more than you realize.
And do not keep Gospel truth trapped behind your screen.
Come to Jesus.
Not merely to an experience.
Not to a denomination.
Not to a manifestation.
Not to an argument.
To Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the grace you cannot earn.
Let Christ forgive what shame keeps replaying.
Let Him expose what religion taught you to hide.
Let Him rewrite what sin tried to destroy.
Because the greatest evidence that God has touched your life will never be how mysterious your words sound.
It will be that your life increasingly sounds like Jesus.
And long after every tongue has fallen silent, the voice that will matter most is the voice of the Savior who called you by name.
